findings.title: has_global_access used as admin authorization gate
findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` treats any member with global/open-membership access as an "authorized administrator" and unlocks the OptimizedCursorPaginator's unchecked negative-offset path. `has_global_access` only means the member can see all teams in the org; it is not an admin/privilege flag. This grants ordinary members a non-standard pagination code path that deliberately bypasses offset bounds checks. The gate should be an explicit permission check (or the feature removed).

findings.title: organization_context.member can be None -> AttributeError
findings.body: For a superuser or staff user who is not a member of the organization, `organization_context.member` is None, so `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises AttributeError and returns a 500. Because Python evaluates `or` left-to-right the superuser case short-circuits, but any non-member non-superuser request reaching this line (e.g. via org-level permission grants or token auth where member is None) crashes. Guard with `organization_context.member and ...`.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with the datetime sort key
findings.body: The endpoint orders by `-datetime` and uses `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, whose `get_item_key` does `math.floor(getattr(item, 'datetime'))` and whose `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value. `math.floor()` on a `datetime` raises TypeError, and the raw int cursor value cannot be compared against a datetime column in `build_queryset`. Any request with `?optimized_pagination=true` from an eligible user will 500 (or produce a bad SQL comparison). A DateTimePaginator-style key conversion is required.

findings.title: Negative slice start on a QuerySet raises ValueError
findings.body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0`, `start_offset` is negative and `queryset[start_offset:stop]` is evaluated. Django QuerySets explicitly reject negative indexing (`ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.`), so a client-supplied negative cursor offset produces an unhandled 500 instead of a 400. The comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong.

findings.title: Silently clamping offset hides invalid cursors and breaks drop-extra logic
findings.body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` silently clamps a negative forward offset to 0 instead of surfacing an error, so a malformed/attacker-supplied cursor now returns page 1 data rather than being rejected. Worse, the subsequent check at line 192 still uses the unclamped `offset` (`len(results) == offset + limit + extra`), so when offset is clamped the extra-row trimming comparison is computed against a different window size than was fetched, producing wrong has-more/trimming behavior. For `is_prev` the negative offset is still passed through to the slice and will raise ValueError from Django.

findings.title: Duplicate trimming logic uses unclamped offset
findings.body: `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` in OptimizedCursorPaginator compares the result count against a window computed from the raw `cursor.offset`, while the slice actually used `start_offset` (clamped, or negative). When these differ the extra prev-row is not dropped (or is dropped incorrectly), yielding duplicated/missing rows across pages. This whole method is a copy-paste of BasePaginator.get_result and should delegate instead of duplicating the logic.

findings.title: No tests for new OptimizedCursorPaginator or clamping behavior
findings.body: A new public paginator class plus a behavioral change to BasePaginator.get_result offset handling are added with no accompanying tests. There is no coverage for negative offsets, the clamping branch, or the new endpoint query parameter, so the ValueError/TypeError crashes described above would not be caught by CI.
